source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
source.authors: Lyzander Marciano Andrylie; Inaya Rahmanisa; Mahardika Krisna Ihsani; A. Wicaksono; H. Wibowo; Alham Fikri Aji

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE dictionaries recover meaningful sparse features in multilingual LLMs, extending the feature-recovery question to language-specific concepts in LLMs rather than toy networks.
record.gate_note: The study identifies features using stated activation-probability thresholds (including the >10% token and 98% example criteria); these selection criteria are not outcomes. The text reports feature counts, layer distributions, interpretation scores, and language-identification results. Steering and text-generation effects are purposefully induced; the PPL intervention findings are summarized below as related results, not as evidence that such output behavior occurs without intervention. Per-language generation tables and downstream-task results do not test the named claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study applies existing SAEs to Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 2 2B/9B. It reports whether the recovered language-specific features are interpretable (automated scores against a 50% random baseline). It also compares them against a language-specific neuron baseline on LID and steering isolation. This bears on V4, the claim that real LLMs contain sparse features an SAE can recover. The evidence is weak and indirect, because the work is largely an application of SAEs as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs capture interpretable language-specific features, mostly in middle-to-late layers. Steering these features shifts perplexity and output language, and they support LID comparable to fastText. They add that the features are more monosemantic than LAPE neurons, judged from steering isolation and Llama LID. They also note a bias toward languages with more features, which is worse for the Gemma JumpReLU SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE-LAPE to find frequently active, language-specific SAE features in multilingual LLM FFN outputs, then evaluates interpretation, steering, and language identification. It does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method or measure toy feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that larger-magnitude steering factors increase perplexity changes and language shifts, while higher positive steering factors can degrade generation coherence. LID performance varies by model and language; they associate some bias with feature counts and SAE training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering language-specific SAE features changes perplexity. Suppression mostly affects the target language; activation disrupts other languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific SAE features causally and selectively affect multilingual language modeling.

fits_no_version.finding: Language-specific features concentrate in middle-to-late layers. Features shared across 9–15 languages concentrate in early-to-middle layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific information in LLM FFNs is concentrated in deeper layers.

record.problems: The results cover three LLM checkpoints and do not test completeness or stability of the learned dictionaries. Interpretation relies on an automated LLM evaluation. The authors note potential LID bias toward languages with more features and weaker results for some Gemma-language combinations; the Gemma SAEs were trained mainly on English data. Uncertainty estimates are not reported for the core feature-count, interpretation, or LID results.
record.rows_left_out: Per-language and per-scaling-factor perplexity matrix cells are not listed individually; the paper's explicit qualitative summaries are recorded in r14–r15. Purposefully steered generation results and XWinograd intervention results are not rows because they do not measure an uninduced behavior named by a claim version.

untested.parts: All of it: toy networks, geometry, sparsity transition.
Capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity. The appendix's note on frequency and dedicated features is speculation, not a test.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; how complete the dictionary is.
Completeness, stability and canonicity. Mislabelled cross-language features (e.g. a 'Japanese' feature that fires on Bulgarian) are anecdotes, not a test.

missing.what: Neuron-baseline steering comparison. Suppressing SAE features gives more isolated PPL effects than suppressing LAPE neurons; authors read this as greater monosemanticity.
Interpretation scores fall with LAPE entropy (detection accuracy Pearson r = -0.643; fuzzing r = -0.551), so interpretability depends on feature specificity.
Per-language interpretation scores and the mean precision/recall (0.85/0.64), showing recall is low for many features.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence on V4 is indirect. The SAEs are off-the-shelf and are used mainly as an analysis tool. Interpretability is judged by GPT-4.1 automated scoring. The informative contrast for V4 is SAE features versus neurons, not versus fastText, so rows r7–r12 are rebased on the neuron classifier. Feature counts and layer distributions are selection outputs and are unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature-over-dimension capacity, near-orthogonal overlap, sparsity transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from competition for limited representational capacity, or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-recovered features, not whether features are spread across many neurons. Does not establish that the dictionaries recover all relevant features.
Completeness, stability across training runs or dictionaries, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether represented features are exclusively one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Counted language-specific SAE-LAPE features across layers.
rows.value: 540 language-specific features out of two million across layers
rows.note: The study identifies these as features that are predominantly active in a single language.
rows.check: Selection count from SAE-LAPE thresholds (540 of ~2M features). This is an output of the selection criteria, not evidence that the SAE recovers features.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the layer distribution of identified language-specific SAE features.
rows.value: Most features are concentrated in the middle to late layers.
rows.note: The paper describes this pattern in the text; figure gives the distribution.
rows.check: Layer location of the selected features bears on where language information sits, not on whether features are superposed or recoverable.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the layer distribution of identified language-specific SAE features.
rows.value: The paper reports a trend similar to Llama 3.2 1B, with features concentrated in middle to late layers.
rows.note: The description refers to Gemma 2 generally; the appendix shows separate distributions for 2B and 9B.
rows.check: Layer distribution only. The SAE size is wrong: Gemma Scope 2B uses 65K features per layer, while the 9B uses 131K.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the layer distribution of identified language-specific SAE features.
rows.value: The paper reports a trend similar to Llama 3.2 1B, with features concentrated in middle to late layers.
rows.note: The description refers to Gemma 2 generally; the appendix shows separate distributions for 2B and 9B.
rows.check: Layer distribution only; it does not measure feature recovery.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated generated explanations of language-specific SAE features using detection scoring.
rows.note: Authors report the median across language-specific features.
rows.check: Correctly linked: median detection accuracy 0.75 against a 50% baseline. Note that some individual features have recall as low as 0.02–0.04 (e.g. Figs 54–58).

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated generated explanations of language-specific SAE features using fuzzing scoring.
rows.note: Authors report the median across language-specific features.
rows.check: Correctly linked: median fuzzing accuracy 0.76 against a 50% baseline.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Classified WiLI-2018 inputs using activations of language-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The SAE-feature classifier is slightly below fastText; the neuron classifier is also reported as a comparison.
rows.check: fastText is the study's comparison method, not the right baseline for V4. The relevant baseline is the neuron-based LID, with accuracy 0.617; the SAE value is 0.972 (Table 11).

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Classified WiLI-2018 inputs using activations of language-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The SAE-feature classifier is slightly below fastText.
rows.check: Rebase on the neuron classifier: macro F1 is 0.528 for neurons against 0.972 for SAE features.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Classified WiLI-2018 inputs using activations of language-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The table also reports poorer performance for some individual languages.
rows.check: Against neurons the gain is small: accuracy 0.924 for SAE features versus 0.898 for neurons. English recall is only 0.098 (Table 5).

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Classified WiLI-2018 inputs using activations of language-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The table also reports poorer performance for some individual languages.
rows.check: Against neurons: F1 0.906 for SAE features versus 0.873 for neurons. SAE English F1 is 0.177.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Classified WiLI-2018 inputs using activations of language-specific SAE features.
rows.note: The paper notes performance degradation for several languages.
rows.check: Against neurons: accuracy 0.917 for SAE features versus 0.922 for neurons, so no advantage. SAE English F1 is 0.000 (Table 6).

source_check.correct: state=partial for V4: SAE-based accuracy is 0.917 across 15 languages, with English precision, recall and F1 all 0.000. Neuron accuracy is 0.922.
source_check.problem: No advantage over neurons does not establish absence of recoverable SAE features; the aggregate result shows language-dependent, incomplete success.

rows.note: The paper notes performance degradation for several languages.
rows.check: Against neurons: F1 0.897 for SAE features versus 0.905 for neurons.

source_check.correct: state=partial for V4: SAE-based macro F1 is 0.897 across 15 languages, with English F1 0.000. Neuron macro F1 is 0.905.
source_check.problem: The lower score than neurons does not establish absence of V4's effect; SAE features still identify most tested languages successfully.

relation.reason: Its own results assess whether identifiable, interpretable language-specific SAE features exist, bearing directly on V4.

tranche.reason: Tests SAE recovery and interpretation of language-specific features in a multilingual setting, with interpretation scoring and causal interventions.

source_check.notes: The fastText baselines are correctly transcribed; neuron comparisons are additional controls, not mandatory replacements. English classification failure may reflect feature-count bias and does not establish that English features are absent.
